title: Portable Ultra-Low-Field MRI Versus Conventional 3 Tesla-Neuroimaging in Critically Ill Patients: A Single-Center, Prospective, Randomized Controlled Trial
summary: Patients in the intensive care unit often need a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the head. Until now, they have had to be moved to an MRI scanner in another department together with their ventilator, monitors and infusion pumps. In addition, non MRI-compatible equipment has to be replaced. This transport is laborious, takes time and can be risky for severely ill patients, for example because of circulation or breathing problems or because tubes and lines become dislodged. Mobile MRI scanners with a very weak magnetic field have recently become available and can be used directly at the bedside. However, their images are less detailed than those of a conventional MRI. In the NEUROPORT study, chance decides whether the scan is done with the mobile scanner at the bedside or, as usual, in the conventional MRI scanner. The study compares how quickly the scan can be carried out and how often complications occur. It also examines whether image quality is sufficient for treatment decisions and how the method affects the further course of illness and costs.
conditions: Neurological impairment in critically ill adult intensive care patients with an indication for brain MRI (e.g. suspected cerebral ischemia, intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral edema or other intracranial pathology)

interventions.name: Conventional brain MRI at clinical field strength requiring intrahospital transport of the patient to the MRI suite (standard of care).
Portable ultra-low-field brain MRI (0.064 T, Swoop®, CE-marked) performed at the bedside in the intensive care unit, without patient transport.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Treatment in ICU/IMC
Indication for brain MRI without angiography
Hemodynamically stable or on low to moderate catecholamine doses
Exclusion criteria:
Contraindications to MRI
Emergent imaging needs that do not allow for study inclusion or randomization (e.g. treatment time window in acute ischemic stroke, suspected life-threatening mass effect from intracranial hemorrhage or edema)
Suspected diagnosis requires angiography
Suspected diagnosis requires MRI at clinical field strength (e.g. small brainstem lesions unlikely to be detected by ultra-low-field MRI)
Severe hemodynamic instability
